claim.source_local_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] Fusarium head blight, North America, China, and Europe.
[111] FHB is an important disease in many wheatproducing areas, including Europe, China, the USA, Canada, and Brazil (Parry et al. 1995;X u 2003; Savary 2014).
[112] The disease has been associated with a large number of plant pathogens, but the literature from the USA and Canada mostly refers to Fusarium graminearum (teleomorph Gibberella zeae), while many different Fusarium species are generally considered in Europe (Parry et al. 1995;X u 2003).
[113] In North America, recurrent epidemics have been reported for many years, but particularly severe epidemics have been taking place from the 1990s until today probably as a result of the expansion of wheat-maize rotation and of conservation tillage practices (Parry et al. 1995;M c M u l l e ne ta l .1997, 2012; Dill- Macky and Jones 2000; Windels 2000;X u 2003;B a t e m a n et al. 2007).
[114] Following the typology of epidemics developed in Savary et al. ( 2011), FHB may be considered as a major chronic disease in many wheat production areas of the world, although acute episodes occur on a background of recurring epidemics.
[115] The 1993 epidemic which especially affected Minnesota, North and South Dakota, and Manitoba, led to the loss of 4.25 million tons of wheat, and over $ 1 billion loss in the USA alone (McMullen et al. 1997).

claim.source_local_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] Fusarium head blight, North America, China, and Europe.
[111] FHB is an important disease in many wheatproducing areas, including Europe, China, the USA, Canada, and Brazil (Parry et al. 1995;X u 2003; Savary 2014).
[112] The disease has been associated with a large number of plant pathogens, but the literature from the USA and Canada mostly refers to Fusarium graminearum (teleomorph Gibberella zeae), while many different Fusarium species are generally considered in Europe (Parry et al. 1995;X u 2003).
[113] In North America, recurrent epidemics have been reported for many years, but particularly severe epidemics have been taking place from the 1990s until today probably as a result of the expansion of wheat-maize rotation and of conservation tillage practices (Parry et al. 1995;M c M u l l e ne ta l .1997, 2012; Dill- Macky and Jones 2000; Windels 2000;X u 2003;B a t e m a n et al. 2007).
[114] Following the typology of epidemics developed in Savary et al. ( 2011), FHB may be considered as a major chronic disease in many wheat production areas of the world, although acute episodes occur on a background of recurring epidemics.
[115] The 1993 epidemic which especially affected Minnesota, North and South Dakota, and Manitoba, led to the loss of 4.25 million tons of wheat, and over $ 1 billion loss in the USA alone (McMullen et al. 1997).

paper_assessments.finding: The 1995 review addresses Fusarium ear blight of small grain cereals, including wheat, and reports mycotoxin accumulation in grain under hot, wet conditions. It does not address the North American expansion of wheat-maize rotation or conservation tillage as drivers of severe epidemics from the 1990s onward, nor does it measure nutritional value of food. The two edges are therefore not directly supported by this paper; the shared FHB node is compatible but the local chain is unresolved.

edge_findings.reason: The review describes FHB occurrence, causal organisms, inoculum sources and climatic conditions, but does not mention wheat-maize rotation, conservation tillage, or North American epidemics from the 1990s onward.
The paper reports mycotoxin accumulation in grain, a food-safety/quality mechanism, but does not measure nutritional value of food; broad nutritional-value wording is only partially addressed.

connection_findings.reason: Both edges concern Fusarium head blight of wheat, so the shared node is biologically compatible, but the paper does not establish the agricultural-practice driver or the nutritional-value outcome, leaving the local chain unresolved.

fragments: The disease was recorded most frequently under hot, wet climatic conditions where significant yield losses and mycotoxin accumulation in grain were reported.
proofs.quoted_span: The disease was recorded most frequently under hot, wet climatic conditions where significant yield losses and mycotoxin accumulation in grain were reported.

paper_assessments.finding: The paper independently supports the North American FHB driver claim and partially supports the food-value claim via mycotoxin-related food/feed safety and quality, warranting a terminology refinement from nutritional value to food safety/suitability. The shared FHB node is compatible across both edges.

edge_findings.reason: Sentences 2-3 establish severe North American FHB since the early 1990s and attribute the increasing problem to conservation tillage and maize-production expansion, matching the claimed drivers, region and period; additional co-factors do not reduce equivalence.

The paper establishes mycotoxin contamination causing food and feed safety concerns and quality losses, a specific food-safety/suitability mechanism rather than measured nutritional-value loss; broad nutritional-value wording is only partially matched.

connection_findings.reason: Both edges concern the same FHB disease in wheat; the paper links North American FHB drivers to mycotoxin-related food safety/quality impacts without a compartment or species conflict.

fragments: Since the early 1990s, FHB, caused primarily by Fusarium graminearum, has become one of the most significant diseases faced by wheat producers in Canada and the United States. The increasing FHB problem is likely due to the increased adoption of conservation tillage practices, expansion of maize production, use of susceptible wheat varieties in rotation, and climate variability.
proofs.quoted_span: Since the early 1990s, FHB, caused primarily by Fusarium graminearum, has become one of the most significant diseases faced by wheat producers in Canada and the United States. The increasing FHB problem is likely due to the increased adoption of conservation tillage practices, expansion of maize production, use of susceptible wheat varieties in rotation, and climate variability.

fragments: Losses due to this disease include yield, test weight, seed quality, food and feed quality, and when severe, market access. edge_findings.reason: Paper links maize rotation and unburied residues to FHB and recommends avoiding them, supporting the practice-disease mechanism, but in Narok County, Kenya (2013), not North America from the 1990s; geographic/historical qualifier mismatches.

claim.source_local_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] Fusarium head blight, North America, China, and Europe.
[111] FHB is an important disease in many wheatproducing areas, including Europe, China, the USA, Canada, and Brazil (Parry et al. 1995;X u 2003; Savary 2014).
[112] The disease has been associated with a large number of plant pathogens, but the literature from the USA and Canada mostly refers to Fusarium graminearum (teleomorph Gibberella zeae), while many different Fusarium species are generally considered in Europe (Parry et al. 1995;X u 2003).
[113] In North America, recurrent epidemics have been reported for many years, but particularly severe epidemics have been taking place from the 1990s until today probably as a result of the expansion of wheat-maize rotation and of conservation tillage practices (Parry et al. 1995;M c M u l l e ne ta l .1997, 2012; Dill- Macky and Jones 2000; Windels 2000;X u 2003;B a t e m a n et al. 2007).
[114] Following the typology of epidemics developed in Savary et al. ( 2011), FHB may be considered as a major chronic disease in many wheat production areas of the world, although acute episodes occur on a background of recurring epidemics.
[115] The 1993 epidemic which especially affected Minnesota, North and South Dakota, and Manitoba, led to the loss of 4.25 million tons of wheat, and over $ 1 billion loss in the USA alone (McMullen et al. 1997).

paper_assessments.finding: The paper directly supports the claim that Fusarium head blight causes important yield reductions in wheat: it reports that FHB incidence/severity were greatest with corn residue and that wheat yields were ~15% lower following corn or wheat than soybeans, and 10% greater under moldboard plow. This establishes FHB-associated yield loss in wheat, consistent with the downstream edge. The upstream edge (tillage/rotation driving epidemics) is retained as partial support. The shared entity Fusarium head blight connects the two edges coherently: the paper links conservation/reduced tillage and corn residue to increased FHB, and links increased FHB to lower wheat yield, so the local junction is compatible.

[84, PDF page 5] A key biological feature of this epidemic is that it resulted from the foundation in Europe of an immigrating pathogen species with an extremely small genetic diversity, possibly a single clonal lineage (Goodwin et al. 1994).
[85, PDF page 5] The entire European potato crop was susceptible to the new pathogen.
[86, PDF page 5] In Ireland, it destroyed the main staple of a population that was impoverished in the very harsh context of the Industrial Revolution, in a country where agriculture was in full transition as a result of the end of the Napoleonic wars.

[51, PDF page 8] First, the cereal rusts directly affect food production (Component 1), irrespective of the epidemiological pattern of epidemics – chronic, acute, or emerging.
[52, PDF page 8] Second, acute or emerging epidemics can affect the stockpiles of exporting countries, the trade of grain between countries, and therefore imports and reserves in importing countries (Component 2).
[53, PDF page 8] For instance, the occurrence of particularly severe (acute) leaf (brown) rust epidemics in the great plains of North America may affect wheat stockpiles; or massive stripe (yellow) rust (emerging) epidemics in the same producing area (e.g. in 2000–2005) can affect global trade and the status of reserves.
[54, PDF page 8] As a result, major importers, such as several countries of North Africa and the Middle East, may be impacted.
[55, PDF page 8] Infrastructures enabling physical access (Component 3) may be affected if wheat production is reduced in an area which depends on wheat for its revenues.
[56, PDF page 8] Limited wheat availability in an area of traditional strong wheat consumption (e.g. the Indo-Gangetic Plains), on the other hand, may lead to increased local prices, and as a result, may strongly affect economic access (Component 4), or the availability of food over time (Component 5).

claim.source_local_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 4.3. Effects of crops on soil microbial diversity.
[107] Different crop plantings can lead to alterations in the diversity and structure of the soil microbial community, thereby influencing the stability and function of the soil ecosystem (Hartmann and Six, 2023).
[108] Notably, significant variations exist in how different crops affect soil microbes.
[109] For instance, crops such as corn, wheat, and soybeans exert a more substantial impact on soil microbial diversity, whereas crops like rice and cotton have a relatively lesser influence.
[110] The differences in growth cycles, along with the types and quantities of root exudates produced by various crops, significantly affect the growth, reproduction, and metabolic activities of soil microbes (Iannucci et al., 2021).
[111] Additionally, the high nutrient requirements of crops can intensify competition for specific nutrients in the soil, consequently affecting the structure and function of the soil microbial community.

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 4.3. Effects of crops on soil microbial diversity
[102, PDF page 9] Different crop planting methods can significantly alter the structure and richness of the soil microbial community.
[103, PDF page 9] The traditional monoculture cropping pattern often leads to the excessive proliferation of certain microbial species while inhibiting the growth of others, ultimately reducing the overall diversity of soil microbes (Kunguang et al., 2024).
[104, PDF page 9] In contrast, plant root exudates can promote the growth of beneficial microbes in the soil, thereby increasing microbial diversity (Agarwal et al., 2023).
[105, PDF page 9] Furthermore, specific crop planting patterns may lead to a decline in certain functional microbes, which can diminish the ecosystem functions of the soil.
[106, PDF page 9] Conversely, diversified planting patterns can enhance the diversity of soil microbes and contribute to the stability and health of the soil ecosystem.
[107, PDF page 9] Different crop plantings can lead to alterations in the diversity and structure of the soil microbial community, thereby influencing the stability and function of the soil ecosystem (Hartmann and Six, 2023).
[108, PDF page 9] Notably, significant variations exist in how different crops affect soil microbes.
[109, PDF page 9] For instance, crops such as corn, wheat, and soybeans exert a more substantial impact on soil microbial diversity, whereas crops like rice and cotton have a relatively lesser influence.
[110, PDF page 9] The differences in growth cycles, along with the types and quantities of root exudates produced by various crops, significantly affect the growth, reproduction, and metabolic activities of soil microbes (Iannucci et al., 2021).
[111, PDF page 9] Additionally, the high nutrient requirements of crops can intensify competition for specific nutrients in the soil, consequently affecting the structure and function of the soil microbial community.
[112, PDF page 9] The root exudates and rhizosphere substances released by crop roots play a crucial role in influencing the growth and metabolism of soil microbes, thereby impacting soil microbial diversity.
[113, PDF page 9] Furthermore, the distinct root morphology and structure of different crops can lead to changes in the distribution and abundance of microbes within the soil, ultimately affecting the diversity of the soil microbial community (Zhou et al., 2022).
[114, PDF page 9] The excessive application of fertilizers can lead to the overgrowth of specific microbial populations in the soil, adversely affecting the survival and reproduction of other microbial communities, ultimately resulting in a reduction of microbial diversity (ˇSimanský et al., 2024).
[115, PDF page 9] Traditional tillage practices may compromise soil structure and diminish both the quantity and variety of soil microbes (Gupta et al., 2022).
[116, PDF page 9] In contrast, no-till or reduced-tillage practices can help to preserve soil microbial diversity.
[117, PDF page 9] Furthermore, the implementation of cover crops and crop rotation can enhance soil microbial diversity while maintaining the balance of soil nutrients.
